Having worshipped thus and offered the *arghya* ending with *svāhā*, [one proceeds] to the second maṇḍala—in the directions from the east to the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra; salutation to Īśāna. In the northeast: salutation to Brahmā. In the southwest: salutation to Viṣṇu. In the center: salutation to Nīlalohita. Having worshipped thus and offered the *arghya*:

Having first offered the oblation (*bali*) ending with *svāhā* to Rudra and the others, and having given them water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and likewise having offered the oblation and water for rinsing the mouth to Indra and the others outside, one should restrain them [with these words]:
"For as long as Mahādeva remains stationed, taking recourse to this *liṅga*,
for that long you must always remain here for the sake of protection."

Having thus informed [the deity], having removed the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering), having placed it in a vessel, and having received the command of Śiva, one should approach Caṇḍeśvara, present the *nirmālya*, and say:
"Thus, protecting the substance of Śiva, remain near Śiva;
having abandoned garments and ornaments, the *nirmālya* shall be your sustenance."
O God, as long as you are present, remain present. Whatever has been done by me, whether deficient or excessive, through ignorance— [may it be forgiven].
"O Caṇḍeśa, by your grace, fulfill all of that.

Having thus made this request, he goes outside. Then, having established the patron (*yajamāna*) together with his kinsmen, wife, and retinue in a pure place, he should bathe him with the waters from the remaining *śāntighaṭa* and the water from the pitcher previously installed, accompanied by auspicious musical instruments.
The patron, likewise, should worship the officiant (*sthāpaka*) as if he were Maheśvara himself.
One should give sacrificial fees such as land, gold, and so forth, without any stinginess regarding wealth.
When the guru attains contentment, then he is to be honored;
for if the guru is not satisfied, the practitioner shall not obtain the fruit of that [action].
Thereafter, he should duly honor the guardians of the images (*mūrtipas*) and likewise the reciters (*jāpakas*) and Brāhmaṇas;
and [he should give] to the poor, the blind, and the wretched according to his means.
For as many atoms as there are in the image, the liṅga, and the pedestal,
for that many thousands of ages shall the maker enjoy the fruit of his merit.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and at all sacred fords—
that fruit a man shall obtain multiplied ten millionfold by installing a *liṅga*. As long as the *yuga-liṅga* remains installed, there shall be liberation and uninterrupted prosperity.
Having delivered twenty-one generations of one's lineage— seven born of the father, seven born of the mother, and likewise seven born of oneself— one shall thereafter go to the supreme state.
Whatever realization of the "state of being well-favored" has been understood here by me, [it belongs to] the Blessed One.

"O Lord, ocean of compassion, forgive all that of mine. Having thus offered this request for forgiveness, the patron (*yajamāna*) should honor all those who are distressed, blind, and miserable. Then the preceptor (*guru*), having recited the *Pāśupata* mantra and performed three circumambulations of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), should prostrate and return to his own home.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*) in the *Śivālayanirmāṇadīpikā*. May there be auspiciousness! In the eastern direction is the *Ṛgveda*, while the *Yajurveda* is in the south; the *Sāmaveda* is in the northern region, and the *Atharvaveda* is in the west.
One should place Aghora in the northeast corner of the palace,
the five-syllable mantra in the southeast, and the seed-syllable of Umā in the southwest and the northwest.

Then, the wise man should recite the Śivasaṅkalpa-sūkta or the Rudra-sūkta in the eastern part, as well as "kadrudrāya," "tvamagne," and so forth. [In the rite of worship of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvārcana),] he should recite the Śrīsūkta,
the Pavamāna, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Tryambaka.
The worship of the six paths; the worship of the three sections.

In the portion of Rudra—(l.2) Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Kalā Śāntyatītā. The Tattva: Oṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva. The Bhuvana: obeisance to Anāśritā; obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Anātha; obeisance to Vyomarūpa; obeisance to Vyomavyāpin; obeisance to Ūrdhvagāminī; obeisance to Rocikā; obeisance to Mocikā; obeisance to Dīpikā; obeisance to Indhikā. (l.4)

The Kalās: (Salutation) to Śāntyatītā; salutation to Śānti; (salutation) to Vidyā; (salutation) to Pratiṣṭhā; salutation to Nivṛtti. The Varṇas: Annamaḥ; Ānnamaḥ. The Padas: 16. Oṃ namaḥ. (Line 5) The Mantras: Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ; Oṃ haum īśānamūrdhāya namaḥ; Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ.

*Bīja*: Homage to the two seed-syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*. Oṃ, homage to the two channels *kuhu* and *śaṅkhinī*. Homage to *devadatta* and *dhanañjaya*. Oṃ, homage to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*).
In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu: Oṃ, homage to the digit of Peace (*śāntikalā*).
The Reality (*tattva*): Homage to the Reality of Sadāśiva; homage to the Reality of Īśvara; homage to the Reality of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*). 3.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Soma," [one should worship the limbs]: "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the heart"; "Oṃ sīṃ, obeisance to the head"; "Oṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the tuft of hair"; "Oṃ saiṃ, obeisance to the armor"; "Oṃ soṃ, obeisance to the eyes"; "Oṃ saḥ, obeisance to the weapon. Having thus worshipped the six limbs, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ, one should worship the two jars of Soma with: "Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī."

The *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas* [are purified] with a *darbha*-grass *pavitra* having three blades and two knots, and a long brush (*kūrca*) held at the tips of the little fingers; [these are placed] in the *pālikās* starting from the east. *Oṃ ... vaikatrtanāsanāya namaḥ |* *Vaikatrtanamūrtaye namaḥ |* As for the form of Vaikartana: he has one face and two hands.
His weapon is a golden flower, which he holds in his two hands.

Having meditated thus: "He is golden-hued, adorned with ornaments, and smeared with ashes at night," one should worship him with: *Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Vaikartana*. Then: *Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vivasvat*; *Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vivasvat*.
As for the true nature of Vivasvat, he has two faces and four arms.
O God, [he] holds a weapon and a lotus in his hands, and is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
His garment shall be tawny, and his ornament coral.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Vivasvat," [one should worship] with "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Mārtaṇḍa" and "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Mārtaṇḍa."

The true form of Mārtāṇḍa, however, possesses three faces and is endowed with six arms; he likewise displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and is adorned with necklaces and ornaments.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Mārtāṇḍa," [one should worship] with: "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Bhāskara; Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Bhāskara.
As for the true nature of Bhāskara, he has two faces and four arms;
with two hands in the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra*), his other two hands hold a pair of lotuses.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Bhāskara," [offering] a crimson luster, crimson garments, and ornaments of blue gems; [and then] "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Ravi"; "Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the form of Ravi. And the true form of Ravi is indeed endowed with four arms.

The specific attributes are: a staff in the hand, a rosary, a water-pot, a trident, a noose, a goad, and a lotus; likewise, the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. These are declared to be his weapons, and he wears red garments.
Having adorned the emerald and meditated thus, one should worship it.
(l. 2) Having worshipped in this manner: Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Lokaprakāśa; obeisance to the form of Lokaprakāśa;
the color of Lokaprakāśa is like that of lapis lazuli. (l. 3)
Ten-armed, adorned with the ornaments of the five mudrās and a rosary.
Five-faced, with two hands holding a lotus,
and bearing a trident, a goad, a staff, a rosary, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), an arrow,
and blue and red garments; he is clad in blue cloth.
Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Lokaprakāśa. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] with: Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Lokasākṣin. Obeisance to the form of Lokasākṣin.
I shall describe Lokasākṣin: one should visualize him as having one face and two hands, with his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*), and white in color.
Having thus worshipped [the deity] with the saffron robe and the body smeared with ashes, [reciting]:
"Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the Witness of the World," one should worship [further] with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Trivikrama; obeisance to the seat of Trivikrama; obeisance to the form of Trivikrama.
Indeed, the essential nature of Trivikrama has two arms or four hands.
With both hands raised in the lotus gesture, one performs the salutation with the two lower hands.

[He is] dark-red and adorned with garments; his complexion is dark. Having worshipped [him] with: "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Trivikrama," one should worship with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Āditya; obeisance to the form of Āditya. And the form of Āditya indeed has one face and two hands.
Resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, she holds a lotus stalk and a pair of lotuses.
Having thus meditated upon the form of the Sun as a jewel-ornament, one should worship it with:
"Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the Sun. Then: "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Sun; obeisance to the form of the Sun.
Furthermore, the true nature of the Sun is indeed one-faced and eight-armed.
Endowed with two lotuses in his hands, holding a bell, an incense burner, and a water-pot;
endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and accompanied by a rosary;
golden-hued, clad in golden garments, adorned with ornaments, and consisting of gold itself.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the form of the Sun with special care.
Having worshipped it with "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the Sun," [one should then worship]: "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Aṃśumālin. Obeisance to the form of Aṃśumālin.
As for the true nature of Aṃśumālin, he has six faces and is red in color.
The twelfth [mudrā] is likewise the hand itself, while the other two are the lotus-like hands of another.

In the right and left [hands], he holds a *tomara*, a sword, a scimitar, a shield, a noose, and a goad; [and] a spear, a *bhetāla*, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*).

Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Aṃśumalin; having thus worshipped, [one says]: Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Divākara. Obeisance to the form of Divākara. As for the form of Divākara, it has two faces and four hands;
two hands hold two *bilva* leaves, and the two [other] hands hold lotus flowers.
Clad in garments of saffron and adorned with golden ornaments, [one should worship] with "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Divākara. Having meditated thus, one should perform the worship. Or else:
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, and Ravi.

Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, Trivikrama, Āditya, Sūrya, Aṃśumālin, and Divākara—one should worship these twelve Ādityas, from the east to the northeast, with their names ending in the dative case (*caturthī*). Alternatively, in the *mahāṣṭapakṣa*, one should worship Indra and the other [guardians]. In the *saptapakṣa*, one should worship the seven Mātṛkās. In the *pañcapakṣa*, one should worship Nivṛtti and the others. Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, and having offered incense and lamps, one should immerse the seed-syllable and the vessel of milk with the water from the Moon-pitcher (*candrakumbha*). Then, one should worship the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

*Oṃ sāṃ sauṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Sakalaguha.* Having thus consecrated the mantra eleven times and displayed the eight mudrās beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having offered incense and lamps, one should recite the *Oṣadhisūkta* accompanied by the auspicious sound of the conch. *Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Sṛṣṭi. Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Pitāmaha. Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Vidhi. Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇyagarbha.*

Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Puruṣa. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the one of yellow complexion. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the one born from the lotus. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the lord of Satyaloka. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the Veda, the eldest of the gods. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to Prajāpati. Having thus placed seeds mixed with milk into the *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas*, and having offered incense and lamps, one should establish the presence of the Moon-pitcher (*candrakumbha*) for the fire-offering rite (*homakarman*).

Having offered a bundle of five *darbha* grasses, having meditated upon the fire of the *suṣumnā*, and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should display the three *tāla*-claps, the binding of the directions, and the *dhenu-mudrā* with the five mudrās. (L. 4) Having sprinkled the fuel with the *astra-mantra* and set it ablaze, and having sprinkled all the sacrificial materials—including the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the vessel, the *palāśa* wood, the fuel sticks, and the clarified butter—with the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the consecration of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the fire, as well as the consecration of the clarified butter.

Having worshipped with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā" two [strands] across the *kūrca* strainer in the clarified butter vessel (*ājyapātra*), and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, saṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, to Amṛteśvara, svāhā," one should offer all the sacrificial substances, measuring exactly one *akṣa-śukti*, with the mantra "Oṃ sāṃ, to Candra, svāhā."

Oṃ sāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ sāṃ sīṃ sūṃ sauṃ siḥ, svāhā to Candrāyamṛteśvara. With this, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having offered eight flowers to the fire and having joined [the contents] into the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should present ghee, molasses, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and boiled rice. Having given incense, lamps, and betel-leaf, one should allow the patron (*yajamāna*) to see [the vessel]. Thus ends the chapter on the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇapaṭala*) from the *Ūrdhvāmnāyasiddhāgama*.
Homage to Śrī Subrahmaṇya. (Vāstupūjā—)

Now, the ritual procedure for the worship of Vāstu is stated. Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for the worship of Vāstu. In the middle of one’s own house, having established a sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) in the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇṭapa*) for the installation of the deity, one should construct an altar (*vedī*) measuring one cubit square and two finger-breadths in height. To the east of that, having consecrated a fire-pit (*homakuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit in width and twelve finger-breadths in height, and being square, on the western altar one should consecrate rice, husked grain, and sesame seeds.

Having drawn a lotus, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti in the center. Having placed a jar in the center and having placed jars in the four directions, one should invoke Brahmā, the lord of the site, with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site. Then, in the jars in the four directions: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sṛṣṭi; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Prajāpati; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vedhas; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidhi."

Thus, having invoked the primary mantra, one should perform worship. One should worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). One should perform the invocation and so forth, display the three *tāla* gestures, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), and the *dhenumudrā*. One should offer incense and lamps. To the east of that, on the altar, having sprinkled [the area] with the *astra* mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the sites of Vāstu (*vāstupada*)". One should draw the eighty-one squares. [Reciting] "Obeisance to the Śrī Vāstupada Yantra," one should invoke [it]. One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps.
On the right side, one should fashion the form of a *kūrca* [bundle of grass] upon female *darbha* blades and *tattva-darbhas* within a water-pot.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
"One-faced and two-eyed, with a topknot and wearing a sacred thread... (l. 4).
And [he holds] a water-pot, a rosary, as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
The Brahmayajña is of pure conduct and likewise yellow in color;
he wears white garments, is formidable, and is the dwelling-place of the Daityas and Brahmāṇas.

Having meditated thus, and having sprinkled [the site] with the Astra-mantra for the sake of purification, one should invoke and worship [Vāstu-puruṣa] with: *oṃ hāṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*. Then, one should place [the mantras] on the head, mouth, and private parts with: *oṃ hāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*. Having displayed the Digbandhana and Dhenu-mudrās, and having offered incense and lamps, one should offer a handful of flowers with: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ* upon the eighty-one squares (*ekāśīti-pada*). One should sprinkle food mixed with milk, ghee, molasses, and soup with the Astra-mantra; however, one should not prepare more than a mere handful of food.

In the center, on the nine squares: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ* | *caturmukhāya namaḥ* | *ānandavedāya namaḥ* | *kamaṇḍallakṣamālyadharāya namaḥ* | *viriñcāya namaḥ* | *pitāmahāya namaḥ* | *kamalasambhavāya namaḥ* | *prathamāya namaḥ* | *vidhiye namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped [Brahmā] starting from the east, one should visualize him as yellow in color. Then, on the six squares in the east: *oṃ hāṃ mārīcyai namaḥ* | *kāruṇyāya namaḥ*.

"Salutation to Sasya; salutation to Mukhya; salutation to Sakala; salutation to the Ṛṣis. Having thus made [the deity] white in color, [one places: on the six squares to the south—*Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Vivasvat; *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Bīja; salutation to Aṅkura; salutation to Gandharva; salutation to Deva; salutation to Rākṣasa. Having thus made [the deity] black in color, [one places: on the six squares to the west—*Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Mitra; *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Yoga; salutation to Suvrata.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāla! (l. 5) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Manuṣya! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sthūla! Having thus visualized [him] as smoke-colored, in the six squares of the north: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Budha! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhoga! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kalyāṇa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sāhasa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhīma! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Unmatta! Having thus visualized [them] as red-colored, in the two double-squares of the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Āpa! (l. 7)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Āpavatsa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to [the deity] ...dhyāya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Having visualized them as white in color, [one should worship] in the two-square spaces beginning with the southeast: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Savitṛ; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sāvitra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvatroya. Having thus visualized them as golden in color, [one should worship] in the two-square spaces beginning with the southwest: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indrajā.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indrarāja; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indrapati. Having thus visualized him as dark blue in color, [one should worship] in the northwest on the two-square spaces: oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrajā; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrapati; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrasvāmin. Having thus visualized him as smoke-colored, [one should worship] in the thirty-two squares starting from the northeast: oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Parjanya; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jayanta.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Satyakāya! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahendra! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Āditya! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhraṃśaka! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Antarikṣa! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pūṣan! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidhātṛ! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Grahakṣata! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidyādhara! Homage to the King of Beasts! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Deer!

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nirṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dauvārika. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sugrīva. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Puṣpadanta. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Asura. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śoṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Roga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rāga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mukhya. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhallāṭaka. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Ṛbhu! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Aditi! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Diti! Having visualized them as dark blue in color, [place them] on the eastern spikes. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vidārin! On the southern spike: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Pāparākṣasī! On the western spikes: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda! On the northern spikes: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balipiñcha! Having visualized them as red in color, [place them] in the four corners of the northeast corner. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Carikin!

In the fire-corner wheels: *Oṃ hāṃ pūtanāya namaḥ*. In the southwest-corner wheels: *Oṃ hāṃ aryamṇe namaḥ*. In the wind-corner wheels: *Oṃ hāṃ jambhāya namaḥ*. Having thus rendered them yellow in color, one should worship them with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*. After displaying the eight mudrās beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as previously described.

With the mantra *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*, one should place a bundle of *darbha* grass in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having worshipped Śiva with the syllables *oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ*, and having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should take the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*) into a pure vessel and perform the consecration of the fire (*agnisaṃskāra*). Having cast the seed-syllable into the interior of the pit and ignited it with fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, one should offer it with three *kuśa* blades as brooms. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He has] two faces, twelve eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
He has a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and likewise displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
he holds a *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as well as a vessel of clarified butter, is red in color,
is joined by Svāhā and Svadhā, and is seated upon a goat vehicle.
One should thus meditate upon the supreme and most wonderful form of the fire of Śiva, endowed with seven tongues and possessing a serene lotus-face.

Having meditated thus, one should place [the syllables] *oṃ hāṃ śaviṃ yaṃ* upon the head, face, heart, and other parts. Having worshipped with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and having worshipped Īśāna and the others, one should consecrate [the deity] with the eight purificatory rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*). Then, having offered incense and lamps, having performed the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* water, and having thoroughly sprinkled all the items—the cooking vessel, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the fuel sticks, and the oblation materials.

In the *ājyapātra*—having filled the *ājyapātra* with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ*, and having placed a double-stranded *pavitra* made of three *darbha* blades in its center; [one should worship] with "To the Sun, *saṃ* *raṃ* *rave* *namaḥ*" in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and "To the Moon, *vāme* *namaḥ*" in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Then, having filled the *prokṣaṇīpātra* with water and having placed a double-stranded *pavitra* into the midst of the water with the mantra *oṃ laṃ*."

Having filled the excellent vessel with water and performed the purification of the hands, one should sprinkle the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. During the bright fortnight, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter weighing one *niṣka*, using the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ vāstupuruṣāya svāhā*. Having placed the seed-syllables of the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*), the maṇḍala, and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the center—[the syllable] *ga* [or *ja*?]—and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ vāstupuruṣāya svāhā*, one should join the oblation-flower with the water-pot (*kumbha*).

Having placed [the vessel] on the left side of the yantra according to the clockwise sequence of circumambulation of the site (*vāstupradakṣiṇakrama*), and having sprinkled it with water from the jar (*kumbha*), one should worship the *kūrca* [grass-bundle]. Then, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) as follows: *Oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the heart). *Oṃ hrīṃ śirase namaḥ* (Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the head). *Oṃ hrūṃ śikhāyai namaḥ* (Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock). *Oṃ hraiṃ kavacāya namaḥ* (Oṃ hraiṃ, salutation to the armor). *Oṃ hrauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (Oṃ hrauṃ, salutation to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ). *Oṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ* (Oṃ hraḥ, salutation to the weapon, phaṭ). Then: *Oṃ hām icchāśaktyādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ* (Oṃ hām, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the power of will). *Oṃ hāṃ vāstu...* (Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāstu... [text continues].
He has one face and two eyes, is endowed with hanging matted locks,
possesses two hands and two feet, and likewise has a long body.
A sword in the right hand and a skull-bowl in the left hand;
in this very sequence, one should worship Vāstunātha.

Salutation to Puruṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the Vāstupuruṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the Vāstupuruṣa. Having thus worshipped, for the sake of expiation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva," using the *svadhā* formula. Then, having offered clarified butter, molasses, soup, side dishes, milk-rice, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel leaf, incense, and lamps.

With the mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ icchājñānakriyāśaktyādhipataye śrīṃ klīṃ vāstupuruṣāya svāhā*, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having offered flowers and incense into the fire, and having displayed the three *tāla* gestures, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), and the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should place [the vessel] on the left side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) after circumambulating the Vāstu deity. Having prepared an offering (*bali*) of rice mixed with milk, curd, clarified butter, and molasses, and having made an offering of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and plantain fruits, one should assume a gross form by means of the *astra-mantra*. In the center of that, one should perform the ritual bed for the Vāstu deity (*vāstuśayana*).
In the east, [the signs] Kanyā and Tulā; in the south, Dhanu, Makara, and Vāruṇa (Kumbha); Mīna and Meṣa shall be in the north; and in the northeast, Mithuna and Karkaṭa.
In the southeast, [the sign] Kṛttikā (Meṣa) month; and in the southwest, Kumbha alone.
A bull in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), and likewise a lion and a fish.
It is recited that the Vāstupuruṣa has made his bed.

Having sprinkled [it] with the Astra-mantra, having worshipped it with a single flower, and having kindled it with Darbha grass, one should perform the installation of the fire (*agni-sandhāna*) upon its crest by means of the Agnighora mantra, mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). Having sprinkled the two feet of the Vāstupuruṣa with the Astra-mantra while the attendant is present, and having adorned them with sacred ash (*vibhūti*), a jewel-garland, and a Darbha-garland, one should invoke some spirit (*bhūta*) and at that moment offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*).

The Brāhmaṇa-paricāraka, having grasped two feet of the Vāstupuruṣa with his right hand and taking the vessel for the bali offering in his left hand, should perform a circumambulation to the right of the village, the dwelling, the sacrificial hall, and so forth. He should do this in the east, north, west, and south. Having released the Vāstu at a distance of seven or five dhanus, he should bathe in rivers, ponds, and the like. [He should avoid] where there is an obstacle caused by gods, rākṣasas, or humans.

By the worship of the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*), obstacles are incinerated; of this there is no doubt. This is the chapter on the procedure for the worship of the site (*vāstupūjāvidhipaṭala*) from the *Siddhāgama*, which is one’s own [tradition]. Homage to Śrī Subrahmaṇya.
(The Procedure for the Deposition of Jewels—*ratnanyāsavidhiḥ*:
Having conceived a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) there, provided with a canopy and banners.
Having established the auspicious seat for the deity facing east, the Guru [proceeds] in due order.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before that, measuring one cubit in extent, one should draw it by making nine squares. Within those squares, a vessel should be placed;
in the center of that [mound] there should be a ruby, and in the eastern square (*aindra*) a lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
One should place the *vajra* in the southeast (*agni*), and the *puṣparāga* gem in the south; crystal in the southwest (*nairṛta*), and likewise a pearl in the west (*vāruṇa*);
the *indranīla* in the northwest (*vāyavya*), and similarly a *māṇikka* in the north.
And in the northeast, one should place coral and the nine jewels,
along with flowers, sacred thread, and incense, combined with water and gems.
Having performed the purification through inspection and so forth, one should worship the six seats (*ṣaḍudhvāsanam*).
One should worship Brahmā in the center of the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Having worshipped him preceded by meditation, one should offer incense and a lamp.
One should place a jewel upon the body of the image, combined with fragrant substances.
Having positioned it on the head, forehead, throat, heart, navel, and feet, and having established the two arms, one should worship with the *saṃhitā-mantra*. (The opening of the eyes)
One should offer the food offering of milk-rice (pāyasānna), as well as incense and a lamp;
having worshipped with the eight flowers, one should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Then, having performed the deposition of the jewels (*ratnanyāsa*) as well as the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*),
[he should recite] the peaceful, virtuous, and excellent scripture concerning the conduct of the artisan.
A sacred thread made of rudrākṣa beads, a turban, and an upper garment.
Facing north, one should assume a beautiful posture;
then, preceded by a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should worship Vighneśa accordingly.
One should perform the placement of mantras on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the hands (*karanyāsa*), and then worship the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
There shall be purification of one's own station (*ātmasthānaśuddhi*), and the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) should be prepared.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity with eight *droṇas* of rice, one should proceed.
Having drawn a lotus in the center of that [mandala], with a jar established in its middle,
together with a cord, a coconut, and provided with a tuft of grass and sprouts,
one should sequentially perform the meditation and invocation for the image of the deity.
One should worship the support and so forth, as well as the worship ending with Kuṭilā;
and the worship beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, in due order, just as previously described.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the east of that, the wise practitioner should perform the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and thus offer oblations.
Having offered fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), he should then offer the Netra-mantra in due order.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, one should worship the deity while he is veiled by a hidden cloth.
Having first drawn a lotus-line, one should then draw a black mandala, taking up the craftsmanship and the weapons while recollecting the Netra-mantra.
Having drawn a circle of light, one should establish an even gaze;

then one should perform the common aperture (*sāmānyarandhra*) at the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the anus, the two secret parts, the image of the Power (*śaktibimba*), and the tips of the breasts.
The sight is like a vehicle and a weapon; one should indeed look at the golden needle between the eyebrows.
Having touched that aperture with honey, one should then perform the consecration;
perform the invocation and worship according to the rite of the jar-consecration.
One should cause [the offering] to be placed into the hand of the deity by means of the bestower of the fruit of the oblation;
having joined it with incense and lamps, it should be free from a concealing cloth.
The first is a cow and calf; the second is the sight of a maiden;
the third is milk, cows, and so forth; the fourth is the nine kinds of grain.
(Verse 5) The fifth is all types of grain; likewise, the sixth is a mirror.
The seventh is renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and the eighth is the proclamation of the Vedas (vedaghoṣaṇa).
The ninth [is] the patron (*yajamāna*) of the devotees of Śiva within that [temple];
it is served by all the devotees out of devotion and reverence.
Having first performed the artisan's work, one should then perform the subsequent rites for the preceptor.

Then, following the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the consecration with products of the cow (*gavya-abhiṣeka*) as well as the sprinkling on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*), and the opening of the eyes (*nayanonmīlana*).
Thereafter, the purification of the *bera* [the wooden icon] is performed through rites prescribed in the scriptures: (p.45b, f.70a, *pratimāśuddhi*, *grāmapradakṣiṇam*, l.1) (*pratimāśuddhi*—
) the horn of a crab, a bull, or a cow, as well as the horn of an elephant and the nectar of a deer;
A mountain, the ocean, an anthill, and the roots of kusha grass.
Having taken the eight types of death, one vessel was established;
[the trees were] the Jambū, the Āmra, the Aśvattha, the Vaṭa, and the Udumbara.
One should cause five bark-ash vessels and one [other] vessel to be placed there;
having set out the *kāṣāya* leaf, the *pañcagavya* is deposited.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for each, it should likewise be placed within the vessels.
The sprouts of the palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, jambu, and vaṭa trees.
Having worshipped the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—including the thread, the lid, and joined with the *kūrca* grass and sprouts—one should worship the *saṃhitā-mantra*.
There shall be purification through inspection and other rites; one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having offered the food oblation, incense, and lamp, as well as the *vyomavyāpin* mantra-recitation,

one should perform the purification of the image (*beraśuddhi*) according to the sequence of the consecration rite using a measure equal to the tip of a cow’s horn; thereafter, one should circumambulate the village.
The consecration should be performed according to the prescribed rite after having adorned [the image];
having adorned it with variegated garments, it is embellished with all ornaments.
Endowed with all fragrances, adorned with flowers and garlands,
possessed of variegated radiance, and accompanied by the light of flowers.
With a small broom or a fine seat, one should perform the circumambulation of the village from behind;
that moment of transition (*caralagna*) must be made the "fivefold purity" (*śuddhipañcaka*) for the consecration in water (*jalādhivāsana*).
Having reached the path of the deities, perform the sweeping of the path.
It was supported by plantain trunks and adorned with arches and banners.
The water was completely filled in the pathways cleared of grass;
likewise, there were jhallarīs, bhramarīs, paṭahas, and maddalas.
With the great sound of the five musical instruments, accompanied by feathered whisks,
and joined with parasols and banners, one should indeed offer incense through the path of devotion.
It was provided with many lamps, accompanied by various musical instruments,
joined with diverse songs, and adorned with every kind of ornament.
One should cause Brahmins endowed with the four Vedas to be proclaimed there;
[the officiating] Ācārya on the right side of the king, and others on the left side.
Accompanied by the Rudrakanyā, the Gāndharva [rite] should be performed before Śiva;
having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should likewise perform the ritual consecration in water (*jalādhivāsana*).
(*Jalādhivāsana*)
Having established the deity on the bank of the water— specifically at the ocean, a river, or a pond— facing the east,
one should perform the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) mantra, preceded by the ritual of formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
The installation of the jar (kumbha-sthāpana) should be performed; one should worship according to the sequence of the ritual procedure.
Having performed the invocation of that image according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings as ritual services following the lineage of the gurus.
Having created a radiance in the midst of the water, provided with four pillars,
joined with canopies and banners, and adorned with garlands of flowers;
having placed the image in its center, one should proclaim the sound of "Śiva."
The Guru [should sit] on a seat or even on a wooden plank, or in water reaching only up to the neck.
And one should bring images there with their heads facing east and faces turned upward;
[one should recite] the Namaka, the Camaka, the Śrīsūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
Accompanied by the chanting of "svasti" by Brahmins learned in the four Vedas,
one should recite [the mantra] near the water-pot (*kumbha*) for the preceptor (*ācārya*) according to the prescribed sequence;
one should recite it for twelve days, or half of that, or half of that again.
It is prescribed for three nights, one night, or two watches (of the night).
Or else, one should have [the image] fashioned by a water-bedder during the *brāhma-muhūrta*;
thereafter, having lifted it with the mold, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is performed as before.
Perform the invocation and worship accompanied by the pitcher-consecration (*kumbhābhiṣeka*), along with incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, and other ritual services. Then,
having prepared the celestial vehicle (*devayāna*), [lead the deity] toward the entrance of the temple.
Having performed the ritual immersion in water, one should cause the binding of the protective thread to be done.
(The Tying of the Protective Amulet:
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before the deity according to the ritual procedure for the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*),
having performed the sprinkling with "Auspicious Day" water (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*), and having prepared the general offering of water (*sāmānyārghya*).
One should worship the deities in sequence by performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the limbs and the hands.

Then, one should perform the worship beginning with the *ādhāra*, as well as meditation (*dhyāna*) and invocation (*āvāhana*). One should offer incense and lamps; such shall be the sequence of the ritual services (*upacāra*).
A golden thread, or especially a fine silk cloth (*dukūla*),
or else a cotton thread— these a maiden should collect in sequence.
The ritual service for the nine Rudras consists of [threads] proclaimed to be in the number of nine; that thread, mixed with turmeric, adorned in the shape of a serpent, (l.
2); that vessel is a coconut, as well as betel, ash, and rice.
Having placed two bundles of kusha grass and covered them on top with a cloth.
Then, at the head of the attendants, he circumambulated the enclosure wall to the right,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and drums and by those reciting hymns of praise and auspicious verses.
One attains the presence of the deity through the sequence beginning with worship;
having worshipped the sixfold arising, one should place [the image] upon it.
There shall be purification through inspection and other rites; one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having performed the *saṃhitā-arcana*, one should offer incense and a lamp.
With the *tryambaka* mantra, one should apply ashes and [protect with] a thread.
Having taken up rice in his hand, he should place betel leaf upon it.
Having placed the tip of his hand upon the deity, he should thereafter perform the tying of the *kautuka* (wedding thread).
With the mantra "viśve tvā," he should fasten it on the right hand.
One should bear the fivefold activity of the forms— creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace— just as one wears a serpent-bracelet.
With the mantra "gaurīmimāya," one should place the goddess upon the left hand.
With the mantra "bṛhatsāma," one should smear white ashes [upon her].
Together with the preceptor, she should be held and worshipped with the eight flowers.
One should likewise cause incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel to be presented.
Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, one should thereafter light the incense and the two lamps.
What is called the "binding of the protection" was prescribed after the sacrifice; likewise,
the preparation for the bed (*śayanādhivāsana*) and the altar (*vedikā*) were each established in the region of Vāyu.
Its height is one palm tree, while its width is two cubits.
One should construct or have constructed a secondary altar (*upavedī*) that is square; alternatively, the central altar (*madhyavedī*) should follow the sequence of favorable proportions.
Above that, one should place a heap of grain consisting of eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
half of that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*), and half of that again with sesame seeds.
One should then arrange nine kinds of grain, parched grains (*lāja*), and *darbha* grass flowers.
Upon that, one should place a cloth; this is the procedure for those born from eggs, performed in due order.
The peacock, the cock, the swan, and the crane of excellent voice—
having taken these five, one should deposit them as egg-born [beings].
Upon that one should place a cloth and cause an egg to be set down;
likewise, cotton, leaf-seeds, and the husks of flowers.
One should place the *kulikā* in three ways, the five *upadhās*, and likewise the *muṇḍaja*;
upon that, one should place a cloth made of hair according to the prescribed sequence.
Also, [the images of] mice, domestic animals, bears, and deer.
One should place the five items, beginning with hair, upon the bed, having gathered them together.
Upon that, one should place a cloth and cause a hide to be laid down—
[the hides] of a rhinoceros, a deer, a wild antelope, a cow, and a mouse. Furthermore,
there are three types of armor, specifically five for the bed.
One should place a garment over it; however, that which comes from the left is prescribed.
One should arrange the five [deities] born from the left, beginning with white, red, yellow, black, and those clad in dark-blue garments.
The egg-born is white in form, while the hair-born is red in color;
the hairless-born is black in color, and the left-born should be completely surrounded.
That form produced from the left is remembered as being five-colored;
having worshipped it above, one should worship it with the five principles (*pañcatattva*). One should perform the worship of the support (*ādhāra*) and so forth, up to the end of the *kuṭilā*.
One should perform the worship of the movable seat and cause the deity to lie down;

one should indeed worship according to the prescribed rite and worship the image (*bera*) even more extensively. Likewise, one should worship the Lord of the Principles (*tattveśvara*) and the Lord of the Embodiments (*mūrtīśvara*).
One should place the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantras (*mantra*) along with their digits (*kalā*).
One should perform the deposition of the thirty-eight digits preceded by the deposition of the syllables.
(The Characteristics of the Bed)
Having covered [the head] with a cloth whose face is turned upward and whose head is directed toward the east, one should perform the fire oblation (*homa*).
Having established the *nidrākumbha* (sleep-pot) together with it according to the previously stated procedure,
one should likewise place the *śivakumbha* (Śiva-pot) and the eight *vidyeśvaras* in the northeast.
Having prepared the seat for the evening, one should worship the earth and the other elements.
One should offer the worship beginning with the invocation, presenting incense and lamps;
having worshipped the one with the hanging beard (*lambakūrca*), one should thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
One should also perform the worship of the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*) and arrange the eight flowers.
Having arranged the incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, he should thereafter inform Śiva.
Taking [the offerings] with the *arghya* vessel, he should circumambulate the sacrificial hall;
afterwards, he should perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) and offer oblations according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having prepared the Śiva-fire and performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should proceed;
at the conclusion of the homa, one should meditate upon the Lord and worship Him with the eight flowers.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the rite of installation for the temple according to the path prescribed in the treatises on architecture.
Having performed the smearing with cow-dung in the pavilion intended for the conception ceremony,
one should make the interior chamber twenty parts in width.
One should first omit the descent [of the deity] in the east, which belongs to Śaṅkara.
The second portion is indeed Brahman, while the third is said to be Viṣṇu.
Having established the fourth as Ṣaṇmukha, the fifth is Sarasvatī;
the sixth is Arhaddbodha, and the seventh is Vināyaka.

The eighth is the station of Bhairava, the ninth is said to be Śakti, and the tenth is Bhadrakālī; that state is the deity of the minor [powers]. Having established each in its respective portion, one should worship them with particular care.
One should fashion the portion according to the deity, following the tradition of the artisans.
Having performed the sprinkling for an auspicious day and purified [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of that size and draw it divided into nine parts.
One should worship the nine jewels by the very path previously described:
diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, crystal, topaz, ruby,
emerald, sapphire, and coral.
One should especially deposit gold and the nine precious gems;
upon that, one should arrange the stones according to the prescribed sequence.
This constitutes the most pure ornamentation for the interior and exterior of the temple.
Adorned with banners fluttering in the wind and joined with plantain pillars,
one should proclaim [the gift] with all musical instruments accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
The preceptor and the practitioner should take the images that have been removed from their beds and, adorned with all ornaments, cause them to enter the temple;
having wrapped them at an auspicious moment, they should establish them in a stable position.
One should cause [the practitioner] to fix his gaze evenly toward the intermediate direction between the northeast and the east.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite and honor the foundational elements (*ādhāra*) and so forth;
having worshipped the stable seat, one should fully worship the limbs of Śiva.
One should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel;
one should especially establish these during the rite of the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*).
(*Aṣṭabandhana*)
In front of the deity, one should smear a square area with cow dung;
then, one should sprinkle the mortar and pestle with pure water.
Having worshipped the six seats, one should place [the mortar and pestle] upon them.
The mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity; the pestle has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
Having adorned the mortar with cloth and *darbha* grass,
as well as the pestle, [one should apply] the powder of plantain bark, lac, and *guggulu*.
Sugar mixed with honey, and likewise cotton-seed oil—
these should be made in equal proportions for the eight-fold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*). Buffalo butter, combined with powdered *guggulu*, [should also be used].
One should have a five-fold binding made of cotton mixed with lac;
combined with powder and incense and blended with fresh butter,
it is to be known as a three-fold binding— namely, the binding of both the cooked and the uncooked.
One and a half parts of powder and one part of guggulu,
mixed with fresh butter, should be bound together with rapid pounding.
Having taken the practitioner and the preceptor, one should bind the deity with the root mantra.
Having performed the eight binding rites, one should then perform the consecration.
The preceptor, having performed his ritual bath and adorned himself, is thus ordained;
he is joined with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and his hands are provided with pavitra-grass rings.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the general and specific arghya offerings are prepared; the ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) is likewise prepared.
One should place [the vessel] upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), measuring one cubit in width;
having made five steps [of the hand], one should worship [the deity] in five vessels.
One should worship [the deities] in sequence from Īśāna to Īśa as the final one, according to the ritual rule;
one should perform the invocation and worship, and display the five mudrās.
One should sprinkle the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamp with the *astra-mantra*.
[The five nectars are] milk, curd, ghee, as well as honey and sugar;
these are the five components of the *pañcāmṛta*, for which one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) separately for each.
Plantain, coconut, honey, sugar, and cow’s ghee—
these are declared to be the fivefold fruit prepared as the *pañcāmṛta*.
Afterward, one should worship Vighneśa, and following that, the worship of the gateway (*dvārapūjā*).
One should worship Gaṇapati and Sarasvatī, and in the center, Lakṣmī;
one should also worship Nandin, Gaṅgā, Mahākāla, and Yamunā.
Having worshipped the gateway of the weapons and offered the *arghya* in due order,
one should perform the worship of the mounts and so forth, and display the *dhenumudrā*.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should gaze with divine vision;
therefore, by means of the *pāśupatāstra* through the procedure for expelling obstacles,
one should worship Vimala and Subāhu at the two door-panels.
Having worshipped the Brahmā of the site, one should then worship [the deity] in the southwest.
Having struck the bell, one should cause all musical instruments to resound;
then, facing north, one should prepare the vessel containing the water offering (*arghya*).
One should perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) with the ritual intention (*saṅkalpa*), preceded by the placement of mantras on the hands (*karanyāsa*) as before.
The substance should reside within oneself, being most pure through the indicative mark of the mantra.
One should mutter the *Namaka* and *Camaka* sections, and perform the placement of mantras for Rudra (*rudranyāsa*) and so forth as before.
Sesame, anointment with oil, and the pith of the fruit of the *likuca*.
Having ground the pure *rajanī* [turmeric] and performed the consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should again perform the anointing according to the ritual for the consecration of the water-jars (*kumbha*).
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars and so forth, one should subsequently worship the five fruits and the rest— namely, milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar—
as well as the consecration with sugarcane juice and coconut water.
One should perform the bath with water containing gold and jewels, as well as water with *kuśa* grass and *bilva* leaves,
water with fragrant mantras, and camphor.
In the center, one should perform the pure consecration and place a flower upon the head;
having wiped [the image] with a white cloth, one should especially purify it.
Adorned with clean garments and decorated with perfumes and garlands.
And also musk and camphor, prepared with saffron paste.
One should worship according to the prescribed rule, as well as the sequence for the preceptor.
One should perform the worship beginning from the *ādhāra* [foundation] up to the *layāṅga* [dissolution-limb].
Starting from the collection of the clay, the second stage is the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
The third is the opening of the eyes; the fourth is the purification of the image; the sixth is the circumambulation of the village;
the seventh is the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsana*); the eighth is the binding with protection cords (*rakṣābandhana*);
the ninth is the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*); and the tenth is the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
On the eleventh day, the consecration of the pavilion for Rudra; on the twelfth, the laying of the bed;
on the thirteenth, the performance of the fire-oblation (*homakarma*); and on the fourteenth, the installation.
The fifteenth is the binding [of the thread], and the sixteenth is the worship of the mantra;
likewise, the seventeenth is the naming, and the eighteenth would be the marriage.

Having first collected the clay according to the eightfold procedure, [the worship of the Subrahmaṇya pavilion is performed]. (p.51b, f.76a, line 1) (Regarding the worship of the Subrahmaṇya pavilion:
Now, the ritual procedure for the worship of the pavilion is being described.

Having performed the ritual planting of the foundation-stone (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) for the construction of the palace and having conducted the *vāstupūjā*, one should adorn [the site] with a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), altars (*vedi*), archways (*toraṇa*), sacrificial ladles (*sruk* and *sruva*), the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*), the ten weapons (*daśāyudha*), canopies (*vitāna*), banners (*dhvaja*), garlands of *darbha* grass, plantains (*kadalī*), clusters of betel-nut trees (*pūga*), rows of *kuśa* grass and flowers, fine silk cloths (*dukūla*), *badarī* fruits, hair, body-wrappings, mirrors, pearls, head-ornaments (*śīrṣaka*), and so forth. Then, within the water-jars (*ghaṭa*), the large pitchers (*kalaśa*), and the *vardhanī* vessel, one should wrap grains such as sesame seeds with threads of the colors specified in the technical manuals (*lakṣaṇa*).

Its purification by washing and fumigation shall be performed according to the prescribed rite: having gathered rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, flowers, and *darbha* grass; and having offered water, gems, a *kūrca* broom, mango sprouts, coconut, cloth, perfumes, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other ritual substances; one should spread [the materials] toward the north-western direction. The Guru, having washed his feet and sipped water (*ācamana*), enters the western door of the sacrificial hall, proceeds to the south-western quarter (*naiṛtyadeśa*), and worships Gaṇeśa.

Having offered coconut and other items as *naivedya*, along with incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, and having prayed for protection during the sacrifice (*yāga*), he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited. Then, having prostrated at the feet of the Guru and placed [the Guru's hand] upon his own head, the Preceptor (*deśika*), having adorned himself with new garments, a sacred thread (*upavīta*), perfumes, a crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, sacred ash (*bhasma*), rudrākṣa beads, and so forth, should scatter grains of rice (*vrīhi-taṇḍula*) in their respective places within the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*). In the center of the altar (*vedi*), he should draw a lotus of eight petals using barley, rice, parched grain (*lāja*), and the seven types of grain (*sapta-dhānya*). [He should then place] the jars (*kumbha*)...
